questions.question: A media query @media (max-width: 600px) applies when:

options.text: The viewport width is 600px or LESS
The viewport width is 600px or MORE
The device is a tablet only

questions.explanation: max-width: N matches viewports ≤ N. min-width: N matches ≥ N (used in mobile-first).

questions.question: In a mobile-first approach you use:

options.text: min-width media queries (enhance as screen grows)

questions.explanation: Mobile-first base styles target small screens; min-width queries layer on larger layouts.

questions.question: You can query features beyond width, such as:
questions.explanation: @media supports orientation, hover capability, prefers-color-scheme (dark mode), prefers-reduced-motion, etc.

questions.question: prefers-color-scheme: dark lets you:

options.text: Apply a dark theme when the user's OS is in dark mode

questions.explanation: Respect OS theme preference to auto-switch light/dark — great UX and accessibility win.

questions.question: Combining conditions: @media (min-width: 600px) and (max-width: 900px) matches:
questions.explanation: The 'and' operator requires ALL conditions true — a bounded range (common tablet breakpoint).

questions.question: A 'logical' media query with 'or' uses:

options.text: A comma (,) between queries — any matching query applies

questions.explanation: Commas separate queries as alternatives (like OR). 'and' requires all; ',' requires any.

questions.question: Why avoid too many fixed breakpoints?

options.text: They create maintenance burden and may not match real device needs

questions.explanation: Fewer, content-driven breakpoints (often via fluid techniques) are easier to maintain and more robust than many rigid ones.

questions.question: @media print is used to:

options.text: Style how a page looks when printed (hide nav, show URLs)

questions.explanation: Print media queries optimize printed output — hide chrome, expand links, set page margins.
